common_name: Red Lake Currant (Classic American Red Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring; Red Lake is a University of Minnesota release and one of the most widely planted red currant cultivars in North America.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch); currants prefer cooler root zones and benefit from mulch. Red Lake is a classic American red currant, released by the University of Minnesota in the 1930s and long the standard home-garden red currant, valued for its long, uniform strigs (clusters) of large, bright red, tart-sweet berries that are self-fertile and productive without a second bush. Fruit is excellent for jelly, syrup, and baking, and the tart flavor mellows somewhat with full ripeness. Because red currants fruit on spurs of older wood rather than new growth, prune to an open, vase-shaped framework in winter and remove wood older than three years to keep the bush productive. Net the bushes at ripening, since birds find currants highly attractive.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production

common_name: White Pearl Currant (Sweet Pale-Fruited Ornamental Currant)

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring; White Pearl is a white-fruited currant, a color form of the red currant species, notable for milder, sweeter flavor than most red currants.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch); currants prefer cooler root zones and benefit from mulch. White Pearl is a white currant cultivar, a translucent, pale ivory-colored color form of the red currant species that lacks the anthocyanin pigment giving red currants their color, resulting in a noticeably milder, sweeter flavor with less tartness — a trait that makes white currants especially good for fresh eating out of hand rather than only for jelly and cooking. The long, drooping strigs of pearly, translucent berries are also strikingly ornamental against the green foliage. Self-fertile and productive, it fruits on spurs of older wood like other red-type currants, so prune to an open framework in winter and remove the oldest wood to maintain vigor. Net at ripening to protect fruit from birds.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production

planting.note: Plant dormant bushes in fall or early spring; Poorman is a classic American gooseberry hybrid bred for milder flavor and fewer, softer thorns than European gooseberry types.

directions: Plant dormant bushes in fertile, well-drained, cool soil in partial shade to full sun (partial shade in hot regions to prevent leaf scorch and reduce mildew pressure). Poorman is a long-cultivated American gooseberry hybrid, valued for combining good disease resistance with berries that are sweeter and milder than many European gooseberry cultivars, making them pleasant for fresh eating as well as pies, jams, and preserves. The medium-sized fruit ripens from green to a rosy red-pink blush, and the bush, while still thorny like most gooseberries, is comparatively less vicious to harvest from than many older European types. Self-fertile and productive, it fruits on both old and new wood; prune out the oldest canes each winter and thin crowded growth to improve air circulation, since gooseberries are prone to powdery mildew in humid, poorly ventilated plantings. Net at ripening to protect fruit from birds.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Currant and Gooseberry Production
